messages.content: You are a careful analyst. Answer strictly and only from the documents provided in the user message. After every factual claim, cite the supporting document id in square brackets, like [doc-2]. If a fact needed for the answer is absent from the documents, say "not in the documents" for that part. Do not use outside knowledge and do not invent figures.

Here are three documents about the Marovale rural solar microgrid pilot. Read them carefully and answer the question at the end.

[doc-1] Marovale Solar Microgrid Pilot: Technical Deployment Report (April 2025)

The Marovale Solar Microgrid Pilot was commissioned by the Santhera Rural Electrification Authority (SREA) and is operated by the Helion Grid Cooperative under a ten-year concession signed on 14 June 2024. The pilot electrifies three villages on the Marovale escarpment - Dembe, Kariwa and Oltano - which previously depended on kerosene lamps, shared petrol generators and a small number of privately owned solar lanterns. Civil works began on 2 September 2024; the first village, Dembe, was energized on 12 November 2024, Kariwa followed on 3 December 2024, and Oltano completed the rollout on 21 January 2025.

Generation capacity totals 184 kWp of monocrystalline photovoltaics: 84 kWp at Dembe, 62 kWp at Kariwa and 38 kWp at Oltano, built from 545 W Solmara HX-545 modules on galvanized ground-mount tables tilted at 12 degrees. Energy storage uses lithium iron phosphate battery banks with 412 kWh of usable capacity across the sites - 180 kWh at Dembe, 140 kWh at Kariwa and 92 kWh at Oltano - operated between 15% and 95% state of charge to protect cycle life. Power conversion runs through fourteen Voltrex RS-40 hybrid inverters with a rated efficiency of 96.2%, configured for grid-forming operation with seamless transfer. Each village keeps a 60 kVA diesel generator strictly as backup; the design caps diesel at 4% of annual energy delivered, and the concession's fuel budget is sized to that cap.

The distribution network comprises 11.4 kilometres of insulated aerial bundled conductor at 400/230 V on 163 poles, with street lighting at 47 points. The pilot serves 657 metered connections: 611 households, 37 commercial premises - including two maize mills, four welding shops and six cold stores - and 9 institutional connections, among them the Kariwa health clinic and two primary schools. Every connection carries a Helion M2 prepaid smart meter reporting half-hourly readings over a 2.4 GHz mesh to a village gateway; site telemetry, alarms and generation data flow to Helion's Osprey SCADA platform, which stores one-minute resolution data from the inverters and battery management systems.

The concession agreement fixes four service targets. System availability must reach at least 97.5% per village per year, measured at the feeder head. Average delivered energy should reach 4.9 kWh per connection per day at full subscription, expected by month 18. Voltage must stay within plus or minus 6% of nominal 230 V at the customer terminals, and fault response must average under 6 hours from alarm to crew on site.

Six technicians recruited from the three villages completed a nine-week training program at the SREA academy in Port Elthing covering array maintenance, battery-room safety, meter provisioning and basic protection testing. Routine operations call for panel washing every three weeks in the dry season, monthly thermal inspection of the battery rooms, and quarterly secondary-injection tests of the feeder protection relays. Spare holdings at commissioning included two RS-40 power stages, forty meters and one drum of conductor; inverter control boards were deliberately excluded from village stock and are held centrally by Helion in Port Elthing. The report closes with two engineering reservations: the Kariwa feeder serving the rice mill was energized with a provisional protection setting pending a load study, and firmware version 4.11 on the RS-40 fleet had not yet received the vendor's grid-forming patch at the time of writing.

[doc-2] Marovale Pilot: Financing Structure and Tariff Design Evaluation (June 2025)

This evaluation was prepared by the Cardamine Development Fund (CDF), the pilot's lead financier, for the June 2025 meeting of the program steering committee. Total capital expenditure closed at 1.86 million USD against a budget of 1.94 million: 0.79 million for Dembe, 0.61 million for Kariwa and 0.46 million for Oltano, equivalent to roughly 2,830 USD per connection. The funding stack combines a 62% CDF grant, a 28% concessional loan from the Santhera Infrastructure Bank at 3.1% interest over 12 years with a two-year grace period, and 10% community equity contributed largely as trenching labor and locally sourced aggregate. Only 6.2% of the 9% contingency provision was drawn, chiefly for a redesign of the Oltano river crossing.

The tariff schedule was approved by the National Energy Regulator on 30 October 2024. Residential customers pay a lifeline rate of 0.19 USD per kWh for the first 8 kWh each month, 0.31 USD per kWh up to 30 kWh, and 0.38 USD per kWh beyond that. Commercial premises pay a flat 0.42 USD per kWh, and institutions a negotiated 0.27 USD per kWh. All sales are prepaid through the Helion M2 meters. For comparison, the district baseline study measured the effective cost of shared petrol-generator electricity at 0.87 USD per kWh and kerosene lighting at an equivalent of 1.20 USD per kWh of useful light.

The financial model rests on four assumptions. First, a 95% collection rate: prepaid metering should push collections close to 100%, but the model discounts for meter bypass and gateway outages. Second, an average revenue per user of 11.10 USD per month blended across customer classes. Third, demand ramping to the design level of 4.9 kWh per connection per day by month 18. Fourth, operations and maintenance costs of 74,000 USD per year, including salaries for six technicians, insurance and a spares reserve. On these assumptions the levelized cost of energy is 0.34 USD per kWh, cash-flow break-even arrives in year 4, and the blended tariff sustains a debt-service coverage ratio of 1.21 from year 3 onward. Year-one revenue is projected at 218,000 USD.

Sensitivity analysis shows the model is most fragile to collections and demand. A ten-point drop in the collection rate delays break-even by roughly 20 months and pushes the coverage ratio below 1.0 in years 3 through 5. A demand plateau at 4.0 kWh per connection per day lowers year-three revenue by 14%. Diesel share matters less financially than reputationally: each percentage point of annual diesel energy adds about 3,100 USD of fuel cost.

The grant includes a results-based component: 45,000 USD is released for each village-year in which verified availability meets the 97.5% concession target, with verification against Osprey SCADA records audited by the regulator. The operating subsidy then phases out, shrinking by one third each year from year 3 and reaching zero in year 6.

The evaluation flags three risks. Kariwa's commercial base is the thinnest of the three villages, and its projected revenue depends heavily on the rice mill and two cold stores. Tariff resistance is likely where informal generator-sharing arrangements are entrenched, since households there perceive a lower unit price than they actually pay. Finally, the inverter supply chain concentrates spare-part exposure in a single vendor, and a currency depreciation of 15% would raise the spares reserve requirement by 22,000 USD.

[doc-3] Marovale Pilot: First-Year Operations Review and Community Outcomes Survey (August 2025)

This review covers operations from first energization in November 2024 through 31 July 2025 and incorporates a household survey of 214 respondents fielded between 7 and 18 July 2025 by the Elthing Institute for Applied Economics.

Measured availability since each village's commissioning was 98.2% at Dembe, 96.1% at Kariwa and 97.9% at Oltano. Kariwa's shortfall traces mostly to a single 41-hour outage on 9-11 February 2025, when a firmware fault locked four RS-40 inverters after a grid-forming transition; the vendor's patch campaign, completed on 3 March 2025, has prevented recurrence. Kariwa also logged repeated nuisance trips on the feeder serving the rice mill until its provisional protection settings were replaced on 22 April 2025. Diesel generators supplied 2.7% of total energy across the pilot, but the distribution was uneven: 6.9% at Kariwa against 1.4% at Dembe and 1.9% at Oltano. Average fault response time was 3.5 hours from alarm to crew on site.

Demand reached an average of 4.1 kWh per connection per day by July 2025 and is still ramping; the cold stores and the two maize mills together account for 39% of energy sold. Collections averaged 91% overall: 97% at Dembe, 93% at Oltano and 84% at Kariwa. Actual blended average revenue per user was 9.40 USD per month. Non-technical losses - meter bypass and unmetered taps - were estimated at 4.8% of energy delivered in Kariwa and under 1% elsewhere; a revenue-protection sweep in Kariwa is scheduled for September 2025.

The survey documents substantial community effects. Twenty-three enterprises were newly opened or materially expanded, including six cold stores, four welding shops, three tailoring businesses and two battery-charging kiosks that converted to appliance retail. The Kariwa health clinic reports vaccine cold-chain compliance of 99.6% since December 2024, compared with 71% in the year before electrification, and both primary schools now run evening classes three nights a week. The pilot directly employs 14 people; of the six trained technicians, five remain in post, one having left for a utility job in Port Elthing. Appliance ownership shifted markedly: television ownership among connected households rose from 9% to 34%, and 61 refrigerators were purchased across the three villages.

Satisfaction is high but uneven. Overall, 87% of respondents rate the service better than their previous energy sources. In Kariwa, however, 38% of respondents consider the tariff too high, most citing informal generator-sharing arrangements they previously used at a perceived cost of about 0.25 USD per kWh - unmetered and available only in the evening, but anchored in local memory as the fair price. Requests recorded by the survey include extending street lighting toward the Kariwa market and introducing a daytime irrigation tariff.

On maintenance, the review notes that inverter control boards remain the critical spare: the vendor's quoted lead time is 11 weeks, and the review recommends holding one board per village rather than relying on the central stock in Port Elthing. Panel soiling losses measured 4% in the dry season, within the design allowance. The closing recommendations are the Kariwa revenue-protection sweep, a tariff-literacy campaign timed before the year-3 subsidy step-down, and a load study before connecting the proposed Oltano irrigation pump.

Question: Using all three documents together, assess the pilot's first year against its contractual and financial targets. Specifically: (1) compare each village's measured availability and the pilot's diesel share against the targets set in the concession [doc-1], and state which villages earned the 45,000 USD results-based grant tranche defined in [doc-2]; (2) compare actual collections, revenue per user and demand against the financial model's assumptions in [doc-2], and explain what the deviations imply for the break-even timeline using the sensitivities given there; (3) identify which village best met the combined technical and financial goals and which fell short, connecting each shortfall to the operational causes documented in [doc-3]. Cite a document id in square brackets for every figure you use, and where a target has no measured counterpart in the documents, say explicitly that it is not in the documents.
